extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and philosophy of science; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical analysis of the limits and relativity of human knowledge, consciousness, and ultimate scientific (and religious) ideas, showing why absolute or unconditioned concepts are inconceivable. Focuses on both the product and the process of thought as demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate Scientific Ideas represent incomprehensible realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimate Scientific Ideas are representative of realities that cannot be comprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After extensive colligation of facts and wider generalizations, the 'fundamental truth remains as much beyond reach as ever.' The explanation of explicable things only makes more evident the inexplicableness of what remains behind; both external and internal investigations eventually confront an insoluble enigma.

rubrics_metrics.name: States of consciousness are only knowable by relation to other states
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental affection can be contemplated as part of a series only when represented in thought in relation to other mental states; therefore there can be no truly first or last state of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'last' state must be represented as occurring in an act that succeeds it, which is contradictory. Because consciousness implies perpetual change and establishment of relations between successive phases, recognition of a state requires perception of its relations to previous states — which would itself be a later state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitude or infinitude of consciousness is inconceivable
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot know or consistently conceive consciousness as either finite or infinite in duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to conceive terminations of consciousness fail because such terminations must be represented (not presented) and represented as occurring; representing a termination of one's own consciousness implies a continuance of consciousness after the 'last' state, which is absurd. Objectively (in others or abstractly) similar difficulties arise from the relational nature of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal self (ego) cannot be truly known by reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in the reality of the self is universal but cannot be justified by reason; a true cognition of self is precluded by the nature of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the object perceived is self, the perceiving subject would have to be distinct — cognition of self as object implies a further subject, or the identification of subject and object which would annihilate both. The sceptic's position (that only impressions/ideas exist) is verbally intelligible but unthinkable, because impressions presuppose something impressed and because one still has an impression of personal existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought can only conceive the conditioned; the unconditioned is inconceivable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind can conceive and know only the conditioned (the limited); the unconditionally unlimited (the infinite) or unconditionally limited (the absolute) cannot be positively construed to the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To conceive the infinite as a positive whole would require an infinite synthesis of finite wholes (requiring infinite time); similarly infinite divisibility is unconceivable. Hence the notion of the unconditioned is only negative — a negation of what is conceivable. 'To think is to condition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness necessarily implies distinction and limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness requires distinguishing one object from another; distinction is limitation, therefore the infinite (which cannot be limited) cannot be an object of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because being conscious of something requires it to be known 'as that which it is' by being distinguished from what it is not, the infinite cannot be recognized (it cannot be distinguished by absence or presence of qualities without contradiction). Thus a conception of the infinite involves self-contradiction and the infinite is effectively only the negation of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is inherently relational (subject–object), blocking knowledge of the absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness is only possible as a relation of subject and object; hence we cannot be conscious of the Absolute or know that something is absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To know an object as absolute would require comparing what is given in relation to consciousness with something out of relation to consciousness — a comparison that itself would have to be an act of consciousness, leading to contradiction. Therefore every object of consciousness is necessarily relative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific explanation proceeds by successive inclusion into broader classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding particular phenomena comes from assimilating them to previously known classes and then subsuming these classes under ever more general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: recognizing a disturbed herbage as a partridge (assimilation to prior cases); anatomy explaining why the bird couldn't fly (inclusion in a known causal class); mechanics and geometry explaining respiration and levers by reference to general principles. This progressive inclusion is the method of scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successive generalization ultimately reaches an inexplicable ultimate fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of explaining phenomena by merging them into larger classes cannot continue indefinitely to yield comprehension of an ultimate fact; the most general truth will be unaccountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If explanations are successive inclusions of special truths into more general truths, the most general truth, not admitting inclusion, cannot be interpreted. Thus comprehension must fail at the ultimate level; 'the deepest truth which we can get at, must be unaccountable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyses of both product and process of thought demonstrate the relativity of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: One can deduce the necessary relativity of our cognitions either from analyzing scientific generalizations (product of thought) or by analyzing the process of consciousness (subjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The product-analysis shows successive generalization ending in the inexplicable; the process-analysis (drawing on Hamilton and Mansel) shows that thought is only of the conditioned, consciousness requires distinction/relation, and hence absolute/unconditioned objects of knowledge are impossible. Both routes converge on the same conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical humility: do not equate thought's capacity with measure of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the limits of reason: the conditioned is the mean between two inconceivables, and the incapacity to conceive the unconditioned teaches that the domain of knowledge is not co-extensive with existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a 'salutary lesson' that reason is 'weak, but not deceitful.' We are warned against treating the horizon of our thought as the horizon of being; acknowledging inability to conceive the unconditioned can itself inspire belief in something beyond comprehension ('cognoscendo ignorari, et ignorando cognosci').
